title: Kids Think Math Is Useless and Irrelevant and That Isn’t the Main Problem Here
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer responds to coverage of a Gates Foundation survey claiming the public wants math class to be more useful and relevant. He concedes that much of school math is useless to adult life, but argues that this is baked into general education and is not the real problem. His central move is to invert the complaint: the problem is not that kids find math class irrelevant but that math class treats kids' ideas, intuitions and sense-making as irrelevant. He contrasts literature, history and biology, which commonly ask students what they think before sharing expert thinking, with math, which usually tells students what experts think and asks if they think that way yet. His prescription is a pedagogy of sincere curiosity about student thinking, illustrated with a pattern-prediction task, rather than an effort to retrofit relevance onto the same content.
points: Uselessness of content is inherent to general education and is not what drives math disengagement.
Meyer reframes the survey finding: students disengage because math class shows no interest in their ideas.
Other subjects routinely ask for student thinking before expert thinking; math rarely does.
A concrete alternative is to ask students what they notice and predict about a pattern before naming the algebraic structure.
The summary principle is that kids like learning in classes that like learning about them.
quotes: It is true that the math students learn is often useless and irrelevant to their adult lives. Many students will conjugate radical expressions, simplify rational polynomials, and use the quadratic equation for the first and last time in math class.
This is, in my view, okay. This is part of the deal with most other school subjects, not just math. Consider the syllabus of an average literature class.
Again, kids like lots of things that have little usefulness and relevance to their lives. They generally do not complain about them in surveys.

In math class, this curiosity is extremely uncommon. Instead, students are told “here is what experts think” and asked, “do you think like this yet?” In math class we ask students, “If an arithmetic sequence a + bn describes the pattern 8, 14, 20, 26, … , what are a and b?

One response here is to try to make this kind of math more useful and relevant to a group of students who vary enormously in what they find useful and relevant. Another is to ask, with deep and sincere interest, “What do you think is going on here? What numbers do you think might be coming up? What is a number you think we’ll never see? How could you predict numbers way out in the distance? Could you make your own pattern?
